content: 1. Ethionamide or prothionamide should only be included in the treatment of patients with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) on longer regimens if bedaquiline, linezolid, clofazimine, or delamanid are not used, or if no better options are available to construct a regimen. This is a conditional recommendation against their use, with very low certainty in the estimates of their effect. 2. Para-aminosalicylic acid may be included in the treatment of MDR/RR-TB patients on longer regimens only if bedaquiline, linezolid, clofazimine, or delamanid are not used, or if no better options are available to construct a regimen. This is also a conditional recommendation against its use, with very low certainty in the estimates of its effect. 3. Clavulanic acid should not be included in the treatment of MDR/RR-TB patients on longer regimens. This is a strong recommendation against its use, with low certainty in the estimates of its effect. 4. A treatment regimen lasting 6–9 months, composed of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL), may be used under operational research conditions in MDR-TB patients with additional fluoroquinolone resistance. This applies to patients who have either not been previously exposed to bedaquiline and linezolid or have been exposed for no more than two weeks. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty in the estimates of its effect. Note: This recommendation applies to patients aged 14 years and above. 5. Imipenem-cilastatin and meropenem are administered with clavulanic acid, which is only available in formulations combined with amoxicillin. Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid is not considered an additional effective TB agent and should not be used without imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem. 6. For MDR/RR-TB patients on longer regimens, sputum culture, in addition to sputum smear microscopy, is recommended to monitor treatment response. This is a strong recommendation with moderate certainty in the estimates of test accuracy. Monthly repetition of sputum culture is desirable. 7. In children under 15 years of age with MDR/RR-TB, who often cannot produce sufficient sputum spontaneously for bacteriological diagnosis, culture may be a more sensitive method to detect viable TB bacilli, even when very few organisms are present. However, for children unable to expectorate, gastric aspirates or induced sputum may be possible, but repeating such tests monthly may not be acceptable. 8. Decentralized and family-centered, integrated models of care are recommended to improve case detection and provision of TB preventive treatment (TPT) in children and adolescents. These approaches are particularly relevant in TB high-burden settings and should be prioritized for populations with poor access to existing services or in areas of high TB prevalence. 9. Decentralized care refers to enhancing TB services at peripheral levels of the health system, closer to the community, without replacing specialized pediatric TB services at higher levels of care. Family-centered care is a cross-cutting principle of child care at all levels of the health system. 10. Strengthening country-level collaboration across health-related programs, decentralizing services, integrating TB care into existing maternal and child health platforms, and ensuring routine evaluation of children with common comorbidities for TB are critical steps to improve TB outcomes in children and adolescents. 11. Evidence from systematic reviews suggests that interventions combining strengthened diagnostic capacity in primary care settings and improved linkages between communities and facilities consistently increase case notifications and TPT initiation. However, evidence specific to the impact of decentralized, integrated, or family-centered care models on TB outcomes in children and adolescents remains limited. 12. The benefits of increased case finding and treatment initiation for children with TB are considered to outweigh concerns about overtreatment. However, potential risks, such as undetected drug-related adverse events and insufficient capacity to manage these at peripheral levels, must be addressed.
